summary: Describes the Multicast Address-Set Claim (MASC) protocol, intended for allocating sets of multicast addresses between domains. It was an experimental protocol and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Big networks need to divide up group-chat addresses fairly. Each one claims a chunk, and this protocol is how they claim without clashing.

questions: how are multicast addresses allocated between domains
subtitle: How network domains claim blocks of multicast addresses from their providers without clashing.

tldr.problem: Multicast group addresses need to be handed out between independent network domains in a way that avoids clashes, uses space efficiently and aggregates well.
tldr.mechanism: A MASC node claims an address prefix and sends the claim to its parent, siblings and internal peers. If nobody sends a colliding claim during a waiting period (48 hours by default), the prefix becomes the domain's. Conflicts are settled by comparing claim type, then timestamp, then node identifier.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2909 was published as an Experimental protocol and is now Historic. The allocated prefixes were meant to be advertised in an inter-domain routing protocol so that multicast trees are rooted in the owning domain.

today: RFC 2909 is marked Historic. It was published in September 2000 as an Experimental protocol, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Claim Multicast Address Sets
sections.content:
MASC (Multicast Address-Set Claim) is a protocol for inter-domain multicast address set allocation. A node, typically a router, claims one or more address prefixes for its domain. Each prefix has a lifetime and is chosen from a larger prefix whose lifetime is at least as long, so that prefixes can be aggregated.

Claimed prefixes are meant to be injected into an inter-domain routing protocol (the RFC names BGP4+) where a tree-building protocol such as BGMP can use them. A domain does not need an address set for its hosts to pick group addresses. But owning a set ensures that inter-domain distribution trees for groups in it are locally rooted, and traffic leaves the domain only where external receivers exist.

The design requirements are efficient use of space when it is scarce, hierarchical aggregation, little change in allocated sets, and robustness through decentralization.
sections.plainLanguage: Each big network needs its own range of group-chat addresses. MASC is how a network says "this range is mine" so nobody else takes it.

sections.title: Domains, Parents and Roles
sections.content:
MASC domains form a hierarchy that follows inter-domain topology: backbones, regionals, then customers. A customer domain has one or more provider domains as parents, and at the top a sparse mesh of Top-Level Domains shares the global multicast space. As in BGP, MASC connections are locally configured, and all of them run over TCP.

With respect to each remote node, the local node has exactly one role: INTERNAL_PEER (same domain), CHILD (a customer that may obtain space from the remote node), PARENT (a provider), or SIBLING (no customer-provider relationship).

Each domain has a managed set (everything it has claimed) and a locally-allocated set (the part its own allocation servers may use). For a leaf domain the two are identical. Prefixes are active or deprecated, and a deprecated one is a parent's hint that it will stop using the prefix after its lifetime ends. MASC can also sub-allocate within a divisible administrative scope zone.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks are arranged like a family tree. Children ask their parents for part of the address range, and brothers and sisters tell each other what they picked.

sections.title: The Claim-Collide Procedure
sections.content:
The RFC chose claim-collide over query-response because query-response would need synchronized replicas of the MASC node in parent domains, and collisions would still have to be handled.

A node decides locally what prefix to claim, then sends a NEW_CLAIM after a random delay below the initiate-claim delay (default 600 seconds). The claim goes to a parent, siblings with the same parent, and internal peers, and a claim timer starts. If a colliding claim arrives, the two are compared and the loser picks a different prefix. If the timer expires with no loss, the prefix is allocated to the domain. The node then announces it with PREFIX_IN_USE, injects it into the G-RIB, and sends PREFIX_MANAGED to children and internal peers.

Claims are compared first by type, in the order PREFIX_IN_USE > CLAIM_DENIED > CLAIM_TO_EXPAND > NEW_CLAIM. Equal types are compared by timestamp, where the earliest wins, then by the smaller Origin Node Identifier.

Renewing a claim or expanding a prefix uses the same procedure with a CLAIM_TO_EXPAND. A prefix with no allocated sub-ranges can be released early with a WITHDRAW message.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout "I want this block!" and wait a long time. If nobody else shouts for the same block, it is yours. If two people shout together, the one who shouted first wins.

sections.title: Messages and Constants
sections.content:
Every message starts with a 4-octet header holding a 2-octet Length (at most 4096), a Type and a Reserved octet. The types are OPEN (1), UPDATE (2), NOTIFICATION (3) and KEEPALIVE (4). The structure resembles BGP.

An OPEN carries the version (currently 1), address family, the sender's proposed role, hold time, and the sender's domain, node and parent identifiers. An UPDATE carries one or more attributes: PREFIX_IN_USE (0), CLAIM_DENIED (1), CLAIM_TO_EXPAND (2), NEW_CLAIM (3), PREFIX_MANAGED (4) and WITHDRAW (5). A claim holds a timestamp, a lifetime, a holdtime, the origin identifiers, and the address and mask. A KEEPALIVE is just the header, 4 octets long.

MASC listens on TCP port 2587. Defaults are a 48-hour waiting period and a 240-second hold time. Errors are reported with NOTIFICATION messages, and the protocol includes a finite state machine for connections and version negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: MASC peers talk with a few short kinds of notes: hello, here is what I claim, are you still there, and something went wrong.

sections.title: Operations and Clashes
sections.content:
A node should connect to parents before siblings at boot so it learns its parents' identifiers and prefixes. A domain acts as a leaf until it receives an update from a child, then it must switch to non-leaf mode.

Timestamps decide collisions and also how long claims are cached. Clock skew could make a claim expire too early, so the RFC suggests keeping updates longer than the Claim Holdtime, for example an extra 24 hours to cover up to 24 hours of skew.

If a clashing PREFIX_IN_USE from a sibling overlaps a local prefix, the same comparison picks a winner, and the loser withdraws the overlapping range with a WITHDRAW so the G-RIB has no ambiguous entries. A node must use either manual or automatic clash resolution. Because border routers often lack stable storage, important state is stored in the domain's allocation servers.
sections.plainLanguage: If two networks end up with the same block by mistake, the one that claimed it later gives it back and picks another.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IPsec can protect each session between two MASC peers. Because updates are stored and forwarded, though, an untrustworthy node attached anywhere in the topology could inject malicious updates undetectably, so each node should peer only with trustworthy nodes.

A single misbehaving node sending many colliding messages could stop its siblings from allocating addresses, but its siblings can identify it and ignore its updates. Multi-address attacks can be prevented by accepting third-party updates only via the common parent domain, with parents accepting child updates only through an internal peer or directly from the child whose identifier matches the origin.
sections.plainLanguage: If a bad network joins the family, it could send fake notes. So each network should only talk to ones it trusts.

messages.label: NEW_CLAIM
messages.note: Sent after a random delay; claim timer starts.

messages.note: After the timer expires with no collision.

messages.label: PREFIX_MANAGED
messages.note: Children may claim within the managed space.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total message length including header, at least 4 and at most 4096 octets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

items.label: PREFIX_IN_USE
items.desc: Prefix is being used by the origin.

items.label: CLAIM_DENIED
items.desc: The claim is refused, probably by the origin's parent domain.

items.label: CLAIM_TO_EXPAND
items.desc: Origin is trying to expand the size of an existing prefix.

items.label: NEW_CLAIM
items.desc: Origin is trying to claim a new prefix.

items.label: PREFIX_MANAGED
items.desc: Parent is informing child of space available.

items.label: WITHDRAW
items.desc: Origin is withdrawing a previous claim.
